implementation_notes: Python's messaging libraries ship the envelope: kombu.Message carries body, headers, properties and delivery_info (with .payload as the decoded body), and aio-pika's Message takes body, headers and content_type and hands the same fields to the consumer; the stdlib email.message.EmailMessage is the native MIME envelope (ordered header map plus payload) for text protocols. Wrap at the adapter - Message(body=json.dumps(domain), headers={...}) - and give the consumer only the decoded body. A dataclass envelope is the right fallback when no messaging library is in the dependency set.
code_sketch:
await exchange.publish(
    aio_pika.Message(
        body=json.dumps(order).encode(),
        content_type="application/json",
        headers={"x-format": "order/v2", "x-correlation-id": cid},
    ),
    routing_key="orders",
)
# consumer: unwrap at the seam, hand only the payload inward
async def on_message(message: aio_pika.IncomingMessage) -> None:
    handle(json.loads(message.body))          # message.headers holds the envelope
pitfalls: Acknowledging (message.ack()) before the payload is decoded turns a decode bug into message loss; unwrap first, ack last.
kombu's .payload memoizes the decoded body while _decode bypasses the cache; mixing the two hides that a message was decoded twice or mutated.
Unpickling envelopes (Celery's default serializer) is a code-execution vector: never unpickle a payload from an untrusted producer.
